attribution.note: Zitron's own sentence in his own newsletter.

semantics.note: 'I believe' states his view outright. It is not graded low confidence like 'I suspect', so I read it as a firm present-tense comparison. The drafter's 'likely' modality overstates the hedge. 'Over 4 years' is kept as the spending schedule.

contract.note: Measuring available private capital as worldwide dry powder is an ordinary reading that fits his own discussion of PE firms. Any wider reading of private capital only makes the total bigger, so the choice of reading does not change the result.

evidence.note: PitchBook figure, published Jan 2026 (before the evaluation date): $4.63T of global private-capital dry powder at end of Q2 2025, far above $325B.
S&P figure: $2.515T of PE-only dry powder at June 30, 2025. This narrower subset alone already exceeds $325B, so it backs up e6.

reviews.rationale: Independent data put worldwide private-capital dry powder in Q2 2025 at about $4.63T, more than 14 times $325B. Even the private-equity subset ($2.5T) is far above the threshold. The speaker's own top-10 PE tally ($477B) also exceeds it. Whether investors would actually be willing to fund OpenAI is a separate question that this claim does not raise.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own newsletter.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps his two points: very few non-AI uses, and none of them hyperscale revenue drivers. The fiber comparison is rhetorical framing.

contract.note: The plain reading (limited practical workloads; no non-AI demand at hyperscale) is ordinary. But 'very few' and 'hyperscale revenue' have no thresholds, so how they are read decides the result.

evidence.note: NVIDIA molecular-dynamics benchmark on H100s. It shows a non-AI capability but says nothing about how common such workloads are or what revenue they bring. Published shortly before the target period.
NVIDIA's own disclosure of GPU cryptography tools. It shows another use exists but does not measure deployment or revenue.

reviews.rationale: The packet shows that some non-AI uses exist (simulation, cryptography). It has no data on how widely they are deployed, and no revenue figures that separate non-AI workloads on these accelerators. Nothing here settles either 'very few' or 'no hyperscale revenue driver'.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own newsletter.

semantics.note: 'Nor will it send' is a firm forecast, limited to the current relationship and with no deadline. The 90% gate is his stated reason, kept separate from the outcome.

contract.note: Scoring cumulative cash delivered under the September 2025 arrangement fits his words. The early-resolution rule needs the arrangement to definitively end or be replaced, which is a reasonable bar.

evidence.note: Joint announcement setting up the arrangement: up to $100B, paid as each gigawatt is deployed. It shows the relationship exists but says nothing about the outcome or an exact 90% gate.
OpenAI's own disclosure of a $30B NVIDIA investment in a Feb 2026 round. The contract rules that a smaller round alone is not enough, and it does not end the September deal.
Huang is quoted saying $100B is 'probably not in the cards'. That is hedged and does not definitively end the arrangement, so the early-resolution rule is not met.

reviews.rationale: No deadline was stated. The evidence points toward less than $100B: a $30B investment, and Huang calling $100B probably off. But nothing in the packet definitively ends or replaces the original arrangement or fixes a final amount, which the contract requires for early resolution. The 90% gate as the cause is also unverified.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words. He rejects a media narrative he attributes to Amodei and others; that narrative is not his claim.

semantics.note: The core claim is causal: AI replacement is not why engineers struggle to find work. The proposition drops the rhetoric about deceit and about the whole media, which is appropriate.

contract.note: Reading 'lie' as 'a false causal explanation' and asking whether AI contributed materially is an ordinary reading. Whether he meant 'not the main cause' or 'no material contribution' could change the result.

evidence.note: TIME, Aug 2025: young workers in exposed jobs, including software engineering, saw a relative employment decline. The researchers stopped short of claiming causation. This neither confirms nor refutes the claim.
Aug 2026 revision of the paper, covering data through June 2026. It calls its findings descriptive, not causal, and covers a later period than the claim.

reviews.rationale: The packet shows employment declines among early-career workers in exposed jobs that are consistent with AI displacement. But the researchers explicitly say causation is not established. No admitted evidence shows that AI was, or was not, a material cause of software-engineer hiring difficulties by Sept 2025.
